blocks.content: OOMKilled means a container exceeded its memory limit and was killed outright, exactly the incompressible-resource behavior covered in the Namespaces & Resource Management module's Memory Requests topic.
1. Recapping Why This Happens at All
blocks.text: 1. Recapping Why This Happens at All

blocks.content: As covered in the Memory Requests topic, memory is an incompressible resource, there is no equivalent of CPU throttling, a container that exceeds its memory limit is simply, immediately killed by the kernel's OOM killer.

blocks.alt: No soft slowdown possible, exceeding the limit means an immediate kill

blocks.content: Exactly the exit code convention covered in the Docker Debugging module, 137 (128 + SIGKILL) is the telltale signature of an OOM kill, worth recognizing on sight when triaging.

blocks.alt: The same 128-plus-signal-number convention covered in the Docker Debugging module

blocks.content: kubectl describe pod states the reason explicitly, no guessing required, if a container was OOMKilled, the output says so directly.

blocks.alt: No guessing needed, the actual reason stated directly in the output

blocks.content:
kubectl describe pod my-app
# Last State: Terminated
#   Reason: OOMKilled
#   Exit Code: 137

code.content:
kubectl describe pod my-app
# Last State: Terminated
#   Reason: OOMKilled
#   Exit Code: 137

codes.bash:
kubectl describe pod my-app
# Last State: Terminated

#   Exit Code: 137

blocks.content: There are two real possibilities, and they need different responses: the application genuinely needs more memory than it was allotted (raise the limit), or it has a genuine memory leak, slowly consuming more and more over time (fix the actual bug, raising the limit only delays the same problem).

blocks.alt: Two genuinely different root causes, needing two genuinely different fixes

blocks.content: 5. Telling Which Case You Are In
blocks.text: 5. Telling Which Case You Are In

blocks.content: Watching memory usage over time, using kubectl top or a real monitoring stack (covered in the Observability module), reveals the difference clearly, a steady, high baseline suggests genuinely needing more memory, a continuously climbing trend suggests a real leak.

blocks.alt: A trend over time, not a single snapshot, is what actually distinguishes the two cases

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: OOMKilled means a container exceeded its memory limit and was killed outright, exit code 137, confirmed directly in kubectl describe pod's output.
A steady high baseline suggests genuinely raising the limit, a continuously climbing trend suggests a real memory leak, watching usage over time is what tells them apart.
